published_statement: NOT RE-READ. As HELD by the tree (massform.py:1366-1377, status READ at D65, not re-verified here): 'TABLE I. A decomposition of the nucleon mass into different contributions. ... mass type H_i M_i m_s -> 0 (MeV) m_s -> infinity (MeV) ... quark mass psibar m psi b 160 110 / I have not shown the errors due to omission of higher-order perturbative effects and errors on the sigma-term and current quark masses. The total effect on individual numbers is about 5 to 10 MeV. Thus I have rounded up the numbers to nearest 10 MeV. The largest uncertainty is from the matrix element <P|m_s ss|P>, which could be larger than the difference of the two estimates shown.' Also held: 'the heavy quarks do contribute to the mass term, the kinetic and potential energy term, and the trace anomaly term. However, the contributions cancel each other in the limit of m_f -> infinity' (after Eq.(25), p.5) and 'The quark mass term accounts for about 1/8 of the nucleon mass. About half of which or more is carried by the strange quark.' (p.7).
published_hypotheses: P1 (search-index restatement of the abstract, NOT READ): the separation is in the nucleon rest frame, MSbar scheme, renormalisation scale mu^2 = 1 GeV^2.
P2 (tree-held quote): leading-order perturbative treatment; higher-order perturbative effects omitted (5-10 MeV per entry).
P3 (tree-held quote): inputs are the (then) sigma term and current quark masses, with errors not propagated; numbers rounded to 10 MeV.
P4 (tree-held quote): the strange matrix element <P|m_s ss|P> is estimated two ways (the m_s -> 0 and m_s -> infinity columns); its uncertainty 'could be larger than the difference' (50 MeV).
P5 (tree-held quote): heavy quarks (m_f -> infinity) cancel between mass, kinetic/potential and trace-anomaly terms.

P6 (FROM MEMORY, NOT READ -- to be checked on reading): the quark-mass entry is M_m = (4+gamma_m)/(4(1+gamma_m)) b M with b M = <(1+gamma_m) m psibar psi>, i.e. M_m = (1+gamma_m/4) x (sigma-term sum), a Hamiltonian-decomposition term and not the Feynman-Hellmann first-order response itself; 'b' is then a dimensionless parameter, not the 160/110 MeV entry.

lacked_data: M's hypothesis is PLAUSIBLE for this result's numbers and does NOT reach the tree's conclusion. What Ji lacked in 1994: any lattice determination of the strange sigma term (the FLAG averages, sigma_s = 41.0(8.8) / 44.9(6.4) MeV, are 2010s-2020s lattice data) and the modern sigma_piN tension (42.2 vs 60.9 MeV, 2.7 sigma). He says so himself: the strange matrix element is his largest uncertainty and 'could be larger than the difference of the two estimates' (tree-held quote). Evidence FOR the hypothesis: the modern sigma sums (87-102 MeV; 87-115 MeV as a Ji-style M_m under an unread memory form) lie well below his m_s -> 0 entry (160) and near his m_s -> infinity entry (110), so the row the tree calls its 'largest READ central reading' (17.04 %) is the one most plausibly superseded. Evidence AGAINST it mattering here: the tree takes the MAXIMUM over rows, so a lower Ji row only lowers the printed maximum (0.1719 -> ~0.11-0.12); the verdict 'below half at first order' needs a 466 MeV row to flip, and every datum moves the row the other way. Having the data changes Ji's number, not the tree's conclusion. Caveat: Ji's actual 1994 inputs were not READ, so the attribution of the 50 MeV gap to his strange content is inferred, not shown.
grade_evidence: OPEN because the source was not readable here: all alphaXiv tools returned quota-exceeded (6 calls), and arxiv.org and every mirror tried (export.arxiv.org, alphaxiv.org, inspirehep, semanticscholar, scipost, springer, indico) were refused by egress policy; no local copy exists. The tree's statement ('Table I ... 160 MeV (m_s -> 0) and 110 MeV (m_s -> infinity) ... about 5 to 10 MeV ... nearest 10 MeV ... largest uncertainty ... <P|m_s ss|P>') therefore rests on a D65 READ that could not be re-read. What WAS checked is consistent with the tree: the held quotes carry every numeral used (A1-A5); 17.04 % and 11.72 % recompute from 160 and 110 over m_N (B1-B3); the normalisation choice is immaterial, 0.031 pp (C1); the 0.1719 largest READ reading and 0.2362 margin illustration reproduce exactly (D2-D3); and no plausible Ji row moves the tree's verdict (E1: 466 MeV needed). Candidate hypothesis drifts -- dropped MSbar/1 GeV^2 qualifier, Ji's M_m identified with the first-order response, the label 'b' -- rest on text not READ here (P1 via search-index restatement, P6 from memory), all point AGAINST M's favour (they overstate the Higgs share), and cannot flip the verdict. Not STANDS (source unread; the vintage of the m_s -> 0 row is exposed by later data); not WRONG (no contradiction shown, the arithmetic agrees); not DATA-DEPENDENT for the conclusion (the moved datum moves the printed maximum, not the verdict); NARROWED would need a READ hypothesis the tree drops, and none is READ.
what_would_change_the_grade: Reading hep-ph/9410274 at source (alphaXiv quota reset, or arxiv.org allowed). Then: (i) if Table I and p.6 match the held quotes and the M_i entry for 'quark mass' is the value the tree uses -> STANDS for the arithmetic, with the data-vintage note; (ii) if the page confirms the MSbar mu^2 = 1 GeV^2 qualifier and M_m = (1+gamma_m/4) x sigma-sum (P1, P6) -> NARROWED (the tree drops the scheme and treats a Hamiltonian-decomposition term as the first-order response; direction conservative, verdict unmoved); (iii) if the Table I numbers differ from 160/110 -> a discrepancy in the tree's reading, to be recorded, graded by whether it moves E1 (it cannot unless the entry exceeds 466 MeV); (iv) reading Ji's 1994 sigma_piN and strange-content inputs would make the data move computable through his own formula.
